procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated February 6, 1969 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Revision No. 541 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Pabitar Singh moved the High Court in revision. His conviction under s. 26 of the Act was set aside by the High Court but his conviction and sentence under s. 25 of the Act were upheld.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Pabitar Singh appealed to the Supreme Court by Special Leave from the judgment and order of the Patna High Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the provisions of Section 35 of the Arms Act, 1959, which deal with criminal liability for arms found in premises under joint occupation, were applicable to the facts of the case.

facts: The appellant and another railway employee were in joint occupation of quarters consisting of a bedroom and a kitchen.
A gun was found concealed inside the kitchen.
At the time of a police raid, the appellant was found alone in the kitchen, having bolted the door from inside.
The lower courts convicted the appellant on the basis that he was the sole occupant of the room at that moment and therefore in conscious possession of the gun.
law: Section 35 of the Arms Act, 1959, addresses situations where arms are found in premises under the joint occupation or control of several people.
Under this section, each person is liable if there is "reason to believe that he was aware of the existence of the arms" in the premises, unless the contrary is proven.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the lower courts had completely failed to consider or apply Section 35, even though the quarters were admittedly in joint occupation.
The Court held that because the premises were in joint occupation, the case had to be examined under the specific provisions of Section 35.
Applying this section, the crucial question was whether the prosecution had established facts from which a court could have "reason to believe" that the appellant was aware of the gun's existence.
The Court found that the prosecution had not met this standard. The gun was concealed in such a way that it was not visible to the naked eye.
Therefore, the Court concluded that one could not infer that the appellant was aware of the concealed gun simply because he was using the kitchen at the time.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that Section 35 of the Arms Act was applicable to the case because the premises were under joint occupation. However, it found that the prosecution had failed to meet the essential requirements of this section, as it did not establish any facts that would give "reason to believe" the appellant was aware of the concealed gun.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution had established the essential ingredient required by Section 35 of the Arms Act, 1959, by proving facts from which the court could have reason to believe that the appellant was aware of the existence of the unlicensed firearm in the jointly occupied premises.

facts: The appellant and another person were in joint occupation of railway quarters, which consisted of a bedroom and a kitchen.
An unlicensed gun was found concealed in the kitchen.
The gun was hidden in such a way that it was not visible to the naked eye.
The lower courts convicted the appellant on the basis that he was the sole occupant of the kitchen at the time of the police raid and had bolted the door from inside, implying conscious possession.
The Supreme Court, however, found that the prosecution's story about the appellant locking himself in the kitchen was not reliably proven.
law: The relevant law is Section 35 of the Arms Act, 1959.

This section states that when arms are found in premises under the joint occupation of several people, each person can be held liable only if there is "reason to believe that he was aware of the existence of the arms" in the premises.
The burden is on the prosecution to first establish facts that create this "reason to believe" before any presumption of guilt can be made against the accused.
application: The Court determined that since the quarters were in joint occupation, Section 35 was the controlling provision.
The prosecution argued that the appellant's presence in the kitchen was enough to infer his awareness of the gun.
The Court rejected this argument, pointing out that the gun was concealed and not visible. Therefore, one could not assume that simply using the kitchen would make a person aware of its existence.

The Court found that the prosecution failed to establish any other facts that would lead to a "reason to believe" the appellant knew about the gun. Mere presence in a jointly occupied space was insufficient.
The Court noted that while there might be "very grave suspicion" against the appellant, suspicion cannot take the place of the proof required by the statute.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution had failed to establish the essential requirement of Section 35 of the Arms Act. It had not proven any facts that would give the court "reason to believe" the appellant was aware of the existence of the concealed, unlicensed firearm in the jointly occupied premises. Therefore, the conviction could not be upheld.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the provisions of Section 35 of the Arms Act, 1959, which deal with criminal liability for arms found in premises under joint occupation, were applicable to the facts of the case.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that Section 35 of the Arms Act was the correct and applicable provision because the evidence showed the premises were in the joint possession of the appellant and another person.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution's case in the lower courts was based on the premise that the appellant was in exclusive possession of the kitchen where the firearm was found, thereby attempting to circumvent the specific requirements of Section 35 for joint occupation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution had established the essential ingredient required by Section 35 of the Arms Act, 1959, by proving facts from which the court could have reason to believe that the appellant was aware of the existence of the unlicensed firearm in the jointly occupied premises.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution's evidence was insufficient to prove awareness, as its central claim that the appellant had locked himself in the kitchen was contradicted by facts (e.g., no locking device on the door) and relied on the testimony of a witness (P.W. 1) who was declared hostile and unreliable.
Given the established joint possession of the premises, no inference of the appellant's conscious possession or awareness of the firearm could be drawn from the mere fact of its presence.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution argued that the appellant had locked himself in the kitchen, which demonstrated exclusive possession and therefore awareness of the firearm found inside.
The prosecution relied on the statements of the Investigating Officer and another witness (P.W. 1), despite that witness later being declared hostile, to establish the facts of the raid.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where arms or ammunition are found in any premises under the joint occupation or control of several persons, each of those persons is liable for the offence only if there is reason to believe they were aware of the existence of the arms or ammunition, unless the contrary is proved.
obiter: In cases where a citizen's liberty and career are at stake upon conviction, courts must devote great care and attention to all questions of law and fact.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The prosecution failed to establish the essential ingredients of the offence under Section 35 of the Arms Act, 1959. The lower courts erred by not examining the case from the perspective of this provision, which applies to premises in joint occupation. Given the established joint possession of the quarters, the prosecution was required to prove facts giving reason to believe the appellant was aware of the firearm. However, as the firearm was concealed and not visible to the naked eye, it could not be urged that the appellant would have been aware of its existence simply by using the kitchen.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 35 of the Arms Act, where arms are found in any premises in the joint occupation or under the joint control of several persons, each of such persons in respect of whom there is reason to believe that he was aware of the existence of the arms in the premises will be liable, unless the contrary is proved.
policy_considerations: In cases where not only the liberty of a citizen is involved but also their whole career, as a conviction would lead to dismissal from service, great care and attention should be devoted by the courts to all questions of law and fact to prevent a miscarriage of justice.
